credDeployPage.title: Fleet deployment — {{label}}
credDeployPage.twoPhase: Two gestures, not one. A REHEARSAL opens the real session on every device, checks the account on record and stops before writing; the write is a second, explicit gesture and only becomes available once a rehearsal of this generation has finished cleanly.
credDeployPage.help1: Rotating a credential creates a new generation in the vault and changes nothing on the equipment. This is where that generation reaches the fleet, device by device, and where you can see which switches have actually taken it.
credDeployPage.help2: Everything shown here is OBSERVED: a device counts as carrying a generation only after a second session opened with it. A device meshcraft cannot currently see is never pushed to.
credDeployPage.help3: The run is sequential, one device at a time, one run at a time for the whole controller — switches cap concurrent sessions at four or five. It stops on its own after three refusals in a row, or the moment a write is accepted and does not read back.
credDeployPage.help4: It never creates, renames or deletes an account: it changes the secret of the account already there, and refuses the device when the session enters under a name other than the one on record. A device never reached under this credential is left to the per-device gesture, where you can supply its current password.
credDeployPage.everyoneCarriesIt: Every device in scope has confirmed generation {{n}}.
credDeployPage.notEverywhereYet: This generation is not installed everywhere yet.
credDeployPage.pushIsNotPromotion: Pushing is not promoting. This screen places the generation on devices and records what it read back; it never retires the previous one, which stays valid and is still tried on every login — which is what keeps a half-deployed fleet reachable. It supersedes the previous generation only once EVERY device in scope has confirmed it, and one device never reached is enough to withhold that.
credDeployPage.bucketCarryingNote: Confirmed on the target generation by a session opened with it.
credDeployPage.bucketBehindNote: On an older generation. They keep working — the previous generation stays valid — and they are what blocks promotion.
credDeployPage.bucketUnreachedNote: In scope, never seen under this credential. A fleet run will not guess which secret opens them: use the per-device gesture.
credDeployPage.bucketAheadNote: On a newer generation than the one being deployed — a run happened out of order. Nothing is pushed to them.
credDeployPage.rehearseTip: Opens the real session on every queued device and stops before writing anything.
credDeployPage.writeTip: Changes the administration password of every queued switch.
credDeployPage.stopsBetweenDevices: A stop takes effect between devices, never inside one: a write already sent has to be read back and recorded.
credDeployPage.notQueuedHelpLabel: Help — devices left out of the run
credDeployPage.notQueuedHelp: Every device the run declines is named with its reason rather than silently omitted. None of them was touched, and each stays in the outstanding list until it is dealt with.

juniperSerial.equipmentDetail: EX2200 / EX2300 / EX3400 / EX4200 / EX4300 — soft reset via "request system zeroize" with a working login, or the assisted hardware reset for a switch nobody can log into: the wizard catches the boot window and goes in through the loader (or the EX2300/EX3400 boot menu). Console 9600 8N1. Command set documented from Juniper's own documentation, not yet captured on hardware.
juniperSerial.hardAssistedHint: Power-cycle the switch when the wizard says so, then press nothing at all — and above all not Enter, because the loader's own line is "Hit [Enter] to boot immediately, or space bar for command prompt" and the window behind it is about one second long on an EX2200. The wizard holds the SPACE bar down through the whole boot for you. CTRL-C is sent too, but only once the FreeBSD loader has the console: earlier it would break into U-Boot instead, which is not the way in. It then goes in through the loader ("boot -s", then "recovery") or, on the EX2300 / EX3400 / EX4600 generation, through the boot menu, which takes CTRL-C and no other key.
juniperSerial.warnTitle: Read this before starting — one step cannot be undone
juniperSerial.warnZeroize: "request system zeroize" erases this switch's configuration, its log files, and every secret and private key stored on it (SSH host keys, local authentication, RADIUS, TACACS+, SNMP). It cannot be undone, from the console or anywhere else. Any neighbour that had pinned this switch's SSH host key will see it change.
juniperSerial.warnMgmtIface: The management interface field decides which CABLE the switch answers on. "vlan N" puts the address in-band on irb.N (or vlan.N on the older range) and trunks every faceplate port so it is carried — that is what meshcraft reaches a switch over. "me0" or "vme" puts it on the dedicated out-of-band port instead, which is a separate cable. On an EX2300 the name "me0" is accepted, commits cleanly, and does nothing, so the wizard checks the switch's own interface list before committing to a name.
juniperSerial.warnZtp: A zeroized EX of the EX2300 / EX3400 / EX4300 generation comes back armed for zero-touch provisioning and will hunt for a DHCP boot server, printing "Auto Image Upgrade:" lines on the console. The wizard disarms it first. If the site's DHCP server does hand out ZTP options, the switch may download an image and reboot on its own — the first commit is refused while that is in flight and the wizard retries.
juniperSerial.warnAtomic: Everything else is safe to try: Junos accumulates the configuration in a candidate that changes nothing, the wizard validates it with "commit check" — a dry run — and only then commits, all or nothing. A refused command is found with the switch still untouched, and there is no half-configured state to recover from.
juniperSerial.warnNoDriver: There is no Juniper driver in meshcraft yet. This provisioning brings the switch to a state a driver will be able to adopt — reachable, with SSH open and a meshcraft account on it — but the reachability probe at the end of the run will not find a connector that speaks to it.

lag.modeHelp: LACP (802.3ad) negotiates with the far end, so a miscabled member is detected and left out. A static aggregate bundles the ports with no negotiation at all: it works facing anything, and a cable plugged into the wrong switch becomes a loop nobody notices.
lag.notConverged: not converged — check the far end negotiates LACP
lag.pickMembers: Members — click the ports to bundle
lag.tooManyMembers: This model accepts at most {{max}} ports per aggregate
lag.needsMember: An aggregate needs at least one member port
lag.importedTip: Read on the device; not yet an intent. Edit and apply to adopt it.
lag.vlanHelp: The aggregate carries a VLAN mapping of exactly a port's shape — access with a PVID, or a trunk with its tagged list. In the bridge tables the bond IS an interface, which is why the fields are the same ones.
lag.fallbackHelp: The untagged VLAN a member forwards in while LACP has not converged. 0 is no fallback: the members stay down until the far end negotiates. A VLAN rather than a switch, because the two reasons to want it want opposite VLANs — a server whose bond is not configured yet must land in the VLAN the aggregate already carries, while a socket an installer may plug anything into must land in a quarantined one. This field appears only on platforms whose connector declares it.
lag.builderHelp1: Click the ports to bundle. A port already held by another aggregate is refused, with the name of the one holding it — a port in two aggregates would make the second write silently steal it from the first.
lag.builderHelp2: Applying sends the COMPLETE list of this device's aggregates, because the write replaces: an aggregate missing from it is dissolved. The intent is recorded only once the device has accepted it.
lag.dissolveConfirm: Dissolve {{name}}? Its member ports fall back to individual links.
lag.rangeRefused: Range selection does not reach the aggregates: ⇧ is measured on the physical order of the sockets, and no such order contains both a port and an aggregate. Click the aggregate on its own to select it.

lldp.viaPortId: recognized by the hardware address of one of its ports
lldp.viaSysName: recognized by its system name only — least certain match
lldp.multipleNeighborsNote: {{count}} neighbors on this single port: LLDP frames are probably crossing a switch that doesn't consume them. None of these neighbors is therefore necessarily at the end of the cable.
lldp.refutedByFresher: A more recent reading contradicts this one: the remote port it names is now facing {{device}}. The cable was moved — this observation is kept, because the device really did report it, but it no longer draws a link.
lldp.observedBothSides: observed, and both devices see each other
lldp.observedOneSide: observed from one side only — this is the ORDINARY case: the device on the other end may not speak LLDP (MikroTik on SwOS don't), or meshcraft couldn't name the remote port on its facade
lldp.observedUnplaced: observed, but the neighbor is on no device of this site: it's not known where to place the other end
lldp.silencePlatformUnsupported: LLDP neighborhood UNKNOWN, and it will stay that way: this platform doesn't speak LLDP. Its ports may be cabled without meshcraft being able to tell — at best a neighbor will see it, it will see no one. This isn't a meshcraft shortcoming, no version will change anything about it.
lldp.silenceDisabled: LLDP is TURNED OFF ON THIS DEVICE — it said so itself. meshcraft read its neighbor table over the admin session and the device answered that LLDP is not enabled. Nothing is broken here and no meshcraft setting will help: until someone turns LLDP on, on the device, this switch sees no neighbor and none of its neighbors see it. Its ports may be cabled — an uplink carrying traffic right now included — without meshcraft being able to draw a single one. meshcraft does not turn it on from this screen.
lldp.silenceNotServed: LLDP neighborhood UNKNOWN: this device's SNMP agent was indeed queried and publishes no neighbor table under 1.0.8802. Either LLDP is disabled on it, or meshcraft is wrong about what its platform can do — either way, its ports may be cabled without meshcraft being able to tell.
lldp.silenceNeverPolled: LLDP neighborhood UNKNOWN: no reading has arrived yet for this device, even though its platform can provide one. It's missing an SNMP collector, or the first cycle hasn't run yet — that one can be fixed.

manualIp.subtitle: real connection to the device, then adoption
manualIp.credHelp1: A one-off credential is only used for this attempt: it isn't saved, and it's presented to both SSH and the web interface — you don't have to guess which way meshcraft will get in. To stop retyping it, save it under Configuration → Instance → Discovery credentials.
manualIp.credHelp2: The instance's discovery credentials are also set there: they're tried in priority order, and nothing needs to be retyped here.
manualIp.credHelp3: Attempts stop after two authentication refusals, to avoid locking an account.
manualIp.credHelp4: The details of saved credentials are reserved to instance admins: the controller tries them without them passing through your browser.
manualIp.passwordLabel: Password (an empty password is a value)
manualIp.alsoReadConfig: also read the current configuration (allows import at adoption)
manualIp.notSaved: This credential will not be saved: it is used for this attempt only.
manualIp.webAuthNoHttp: does not authenticate at the HTTP level
manualIp.proxyEveryPathHelp: This probes the address through every path the site has — this instance and each of its proxies — then asks you which one to keep. It does not decide for you: several proxies can reach a device, and the right one is the one that will still see it once adopted. Not to be confused with the serial assistant's "By declared range", which names ONE path from the declared ranges.
manualIp.proxyEveryPathCount_other: {{count}} paths will be tried, one after the other.
manualIp.sweepPickOne: Several paths answered. Choose the one this device should be reached by.
manualIp.sweepNowhere: No path reached {{ip}}. Check the address, or declare a range covering it on the proxy that sees this network.

proxyPage.coverageHelp1: Coverage defines who administers the proxy and for which sites it serves. You only see instance proxies and those covering one of your sites, and you can only add or remove your sites from their coverage. Acting on the proxy itself (revoke, delete, migrate) requires administering all sites it covers.
proxyPage.coverageHelp2: It does not define what the proxy can reach — that is observed. And a discovered device's site is chosen at adoption.
proxyPage.coverageHelp3: Cross-instance migration: first generate an enrollment token on the destination instance, then enter its URL and token here. On its next heartbeat, the proxy enrolls there, rewrites its local state, and switches — nothing to do on the proxy machine.
proxyPage.deployDockerHelp1: The meshcraft/proxy image (amd64, arm64, armv7) is distributed by this controller's built-in registry: generated docker-compose pulls from here and embeds a 1-hour enrollment token.
proxyPage.binaryInstallHelp1: The script detects the host architecture, downloads the matching binary, verifies its SHA-256, creates an unprivileged service account, and installs a hardened systemd unit. It embeds a 1-hour enrollment token and is safe to re-run: an already enrolled identity is not touched.
proxyPage.binaryInstallHelp2: The token is a secret: the script stores it in /etc/meshcraft/proxy.env with mode 0600, never in the systemd unit which is world-readable.
proxyPage.binaryInstallHelp3: Manual start: MESHCRAFT_CONTROLLER (this controller URL) and MESHCRAFT_ENROLL_TOKEN as environment variables. State is persisted in /var/lib/meshcraft/state.json.
proxyPage.renameHelp1: A tracking label, freely editable: the proxy identity is its UUID, not its name. Its enrollment, scan ranges, and access paths are not changed.
proxyPage.coverageModalHelp1: Covered sites determine who sees this proxy, who administers it, and for which sites it can provide access paths.
proxyPage.siteYouAdminTitle: You administer this site: you can remove the proxy from its coverage
proxyPage.siteNotAdminTitle: Covered site you do not administer
proxyPage.upgradeHelp1Full: The proxy downloads its architecture binary, verifies SHA-256, and re-executes. If it does not restart, it falls back to the image binary after two attempts and the failure appears in the table — the Docker image is never touched.
proxyPage.migrateApplyNoteFull: The proxy applies the order on its next heartbeat (≤ 30 s). On failure (unreachable URL, expired token), it stays attached to this instance and the error appears in its logs — the order can be cancelled until applied.
proxyPage.coverageRightsNote: You can only act on sites you administer: others appear locked.

proxyPrefixes.title: Ranges scanned by "{{name}}"
proxyPrefixes.noneScanned: This proxy scans no range. Until it declares one, nothing will be discovered behind it — even networks it reaches perfectly.
proxyPrefixes.networkHelp: Only change the network if this proxy looks at the SAME network as another. Two identical ranges attached to the same network merge what both proxies discover; attached to distinct networks, they stay separate. When in doubt, leave the network specific to the proxy: wrongly separating costs a duplicate, wrongly merging melts two devices into a single sheet.

scanPrefixes.domainCreated: Network "{{name}}" created — attach your ranges to it
scanPrefixes.prefixHelp: Assumed limits: at most 4,096 addresses per range (a /20 in IPv4), and in IPv6 nothing wider than a /112 — a /64 contains 1.8·10¹⁹ addresses, it cannot be enumerated. For a single IPv6 device, use manual IP add instead.
scanPrefixes.domainHelp: The network is what gives an address its meaning. Two ranges attached to the same network describe the same LAN: a silent device seen by both proxies counts only once. Attached to two networks, they remain foreign to each other — as with two branch offices both on 192.168.1.0/24. A serial number or MAC address always overrides this classification: they identify the device everywhere.
scanPrefixes.collisionWarning: {{prefix}} is already declared on {{list}}. If this is the SAME network reached via another path, choose its network above: the two proxies' discoveries will merge. If these are two different networks that share this addressing scheme, leave "network specific to this proxy".

siteCredsPage.caPemHelp: The authority the switch's certificate must chain to. Left empty, verification uses the system store, which on a proxy image contains no switch's issuer — which is exactly why "do not check the certificate" exists. Filled in, it makes that option unnecessary: this is the only setting on this page that actually protects against someone on the management path.
siteCredsPage.caPemNotSealed: This certificate is NOT vault-sealed. Every other field on this form is encrypted and never shown again; this one is stored in clear and returned on every read. That is deliberate: a certificate authority is public by construction — distributing it is the whole point — and putting it behind the vault would cost a decryption on every monitoring computation to protect something that is not a secret.
siteCredsPage.generationCreatedToast: New generation created — previous still valid
siteCredsPage.gnmiIntro: An account that must ALREADY exist on the switch: meshcraft does not create it and does not push it.
siteCredsPage.gnmiLeastPrivilegeUnverified: Use the least-privileged account your platform accepts for a subscription. Whether a read-only operator role suffices on EOS, or whether it really needs an admin role, has not been established on hardware — so treat this password as capable of reconfiguring the switch until proven otherwise.
siteCredsPage.gnmiNotPushed: meshcraft never writes this account onto equipment. Create it on the switch first, then record it here. A device whose site has no gNMI credential is simply not subscribed — silently, device by device — which is why an Arista can stream perfectly while nothing is collected.
siteCredsPage.gnmiPlaintextBadgeTip: This telemetry credential subscribes WITHOUT TLS: its password travels in clear in gRPC metadata on the management network, on every device this credential's scope covers.
siteCredsPage.gnmiRotateNote: This credential is NOT pushed: change the password on the switch first, then record the new one here. Rotating here first leaves every subscription failing authentication, which surfaces days later as "telemetry stopped".
siteCredsPage.gnmiSkipVerifyBadgeTip: TLS is on, but the switch's certificate is not checked. A passive listener is defeated; someone able to intercept the session is not.
siteCredsPage.gnmiWhatItIs: A gNMI subscription authenticates against the switch's ordinary AAA stack — a username and a password, not an SNMP community. That is why this is a credential kind of its own: a leaked read-only community reads a MIB, while this login CONFIGURES the device. Giving telemetry its own kind means a compromised proxy costs a subscriber, not a configurer, and lets this account be rotated without touching the one meshcraft adopts devices with.
siteCredsPage.help1: One credential per site, plus one per device group when password policies differ between models.
siteCredsPage.help2: Revealing a password is logged with your identity.
siteCredsPage.help3: Password policies. Some ranges reject the site secret: MikroTik SwOS caps passwords at 15 characters, and its connector refuses the site secret before sending. meshcraft then generates a suitable password under a technical tag pwpolicy-len<N>, and tags affected devices. These credentials are held by meshcraft: their secret can be revealed and rotated, but scope cannot be changed or deleted.
siteCredsPage.help4: SNMP. An v2c community applies site-wide — read-only: meshcraft never deploys write communities. A v3 identity targets tag snmpv3-<auth>-<priv>. Mixed fleets need as many v3 credentials as cryptographic families.
siteCredsPage.help5: An v3 identity carries two distinct secret phrases: one authenticates, one encrypts. One compromised device in the family exposes monitoring for the whole family.
siteCredsPage.instanceDisabled: Disabled for discovery — still the password on every device it was applied to.
siteCredsPage.instanceIntro: Standard credentials used by discovery — and placed by the serial soft-reset, because the browser has to type a secret on a console the controller cannot open. Equipment provisioned over serial but not yet adopted is reachable only with one of these, not with the site password.
siteCredsPage.keyInDbError: The encryption key is stored in the database it protects (MESHCRAFT_SECRET_KEY missing). A dump leak would expose these passwords.
siteCredsPage.managedScopeTitle: Reserved scope: this credential is generated and held by meshcraft based on what the platform connector declares. Its name and scope cannot be changed; deleting it would leave affected devices without an applicable credential.
siteCredsPage.noCredentials: No credentials defined. Without them, meshcraft cannot connect to devices on this site.
siteCredsPage.noDefaultWarning: No default credential: devices outside groups will have none.
siteCredsPage.noPrivPhrase: no encryption phrase — will not be deployed
siteCredsPage.noPrivWarning: Without encryption: polls travel in clear, only origin is authenticated.
siteCredsPage.noteMaxLenPlaceholder: e.g. 32 characters max on this range
siteCredsPage.perDeviceToast: A distinct secret will be generated per device
siteCredsPage.phrasesMustDiffer: The two phrases must be different.
siteCredsPage.pwPolicyNote: only devices whose platform enforces this password length
siteCredsPage.reservedScopeError: Reserved namespace — choose an operational tag or site scope.
siteCredsPage.reservedScopeErrorDetail: "{{tag}}" belongs to a reserved namespace: these credentials are generated and held by meshcraft based on what each platform connector declares. Choose an operational tag or site scope.
siteCredsPage.revealLogged: This reveal was logged to the site journal with your identity.
siteCredsPage.rotateDeployNote: Creating the generation does not push it yet: deployment is per device with verification.
siteCredsPage.rotateNote: The old secret is not deleted: it moves to retiring and stays valid while devices carry it.
siteCredsPage.rotationCreated: New generation created — previous still valid
siteCredsPage.scopeTagHelp: Prefer tag: a device can carry as many as needed, and tagging rules set them automatically. Group is unique per device and is only assigned via site configuration import — kept for existing fleets that use it.
siteCredsPage.secretNeverReread: This page never re-reads secrets: change replaces, empty keeps.

siteCredsPage.title: Site credentials
siteCredsPage.tlsPlaintext: No TLS — the password travels in the clear
siteCredsPage.tlsPlaintextNote: gRPC without encryption: the account's password is sent in clear metadata, on every subscription, to every device this credential covers.
siteCredsPage.tlsPlaintextWarning: This is a security decision, not a setting. The password of an account that can reconfigure the switch will be sent IN THE CLEAR, in gRPC metadata, on your management network — on every device this credential's scope covers, on every reconnection, for as long as it stays selected. Anyone able to read that traffic gets the account. Choose "TLS, certificate NOT checked" instead if the obstacle is a self-signed certificate: it is strictly better and costs nothing.
siteCredsPage.tlsSkipVerifyNote: For switches with their factory self-signed certificate, at a site with no authority to check against. Weaker than checking, and far stronger than no TLS at all.
siteCredsPage.tlsSkipVerifyWarning: The switch's identity is not verified: anyone able to intercept the session can present their own certificate and read the password. Supply a certificate authority below to close this.
siteCredsPage.tlsVerifyNote: The default, and the only mode that resists someone on the management path. Needs a certificate the switch presents that chains to a known authority.
siteCredsPage.v2cReadNote: read community — meshcraft never deploys write communities
siteCredsPage.v2cRotateNote: For a community, a device left behind simply stops answering polls — it does not become unreachable.
siteCredsPage.v3FamilyNote: only devices of this cryptographic family
siteCredsPage.v3FillBothOrNone: Fill both phrases, or neither: they change together.
siteCredsPage.v3PairTogether: An v3 identity is the pair: they renew together.
siteCredsPage.v3RevealHelp: These two phrases are deliberately different: SNMPv3 derives a key from each.
siteCredsPage.v3RevealHelpFull: These two phrases are deliberately different: SNMPv3 derives a key from each by the same calculation. The same phrase on both sides would make the encryption key only the start of the authentication key — whoever gets one gets the other.
siteCredsPage.v3TargetTagHelp: This identity only applies to devices with this tag: the v3 key derives from the algorithm pair; a device that does not accept them cannot carry it. The tag is technical — provisioning sets it from what the connector announces.

alertingPage.title: Alerting
alertingPage.subtitle: where this site's outages go, and whether that path works
alertingPage.none: No notification channel. This site's outages reach the journal and nobody else.
alertingPage.policyTitle: A port alerts only if someone cared about it
alertingPage.policyNote: Three sources wake somebody: a device going unreachable, a port facing another device of the fleet, and a port carrying a description. A port with neither a description nor a known neighbour stays in the journal and sends nothing — deliberately. On a fleet of two thousand ports, alerting on all of them produces a channel nobody reads by the end of the week. The counterpart is written down: a critical port nobody described stays silent, and the count of what was excluded is shown below so the gap is a number rather than nothing.
alertingPage.slackTargetInUrl: the webhook URL carries the destination
alertingPage.whyExcluded: These ports carry no description and face no device meshcraft knows, so they wake nobody. If one of them matters, describe it on the Ports screen — a described port is a port someone cared about, and that is the signal this policy reads.
alertingPage.wouldStaySilentTitle: This channel will never send anything
alertingPage.wouldStaySilentNote: It subscribes to no class, or its severity floor sits above anything the alerting produces. It will look configured and stay mute.
alertingPage.untestedTitle: This channel has never delivered anything
alertingPage.untestedNote: It may be configured perfectly; nothing has shown that it is. Send a test now rather than finding out during an incident.
alertingPage.lastErrorTitle_one: Last attempt failed ({{count}} in a row)
alertingPage.lastErrorTitle_other: Last attempts failed ({{count}} in a row)
alertingPage.revealLogged: This revelation was recorded in the journal before this window opened.
alertingPage.help: Alerting reads the event journal; it runs no second detection. A port transition is held briefly, and a port that keeps moving produces one message saying it is flapping rather than one per change. Anything attributable to a meshcraft action — an apply, an adoption, a credential push — is postponed rather than announced as news, and re-armed afterwards if the problem is still there.
alertingPage.helpKind: Telegram needs a bot token and the id of the chat to post in. Slack needs an incoming-webhook URL, which is both the address and the credential.
alertingPage.helpChatId: The numeric id of the chat or group. A group id is negative. This is not a secret and is stored as such.
alertingPage.helpBotToken: Stored in the encrypted vault, never shown again. The bot must have been started, or added to the group, before it can post.
alertingPage.helpWebhook: The whole URL is the credential: anyone holding it can post to the channel. Stored in the encrypted vault, never shown again. Must be https.
alertingPage.tokenKeepPlaceholder: leave empty to keep the stored token
alertingPage.helpClasses: Ports with neither a description nor a known neighbour are never alerted, whatever is selected here — that is the policy, not an option.
alertingPage.helpMinSeverity: Applied inside the classes selected above, never instead of them. "Problems only" drops recoveries, which means nothing tells you it came back.

siteExtPage.title: Extensions
siteExtPage.subtitle: the foreign controllers this site is backed by
siteExtPage.help: The token is stored encrypted in the credential vault, like any site credential: it is never displayed by this list, and reading it is a separate action that is logged.
siteExtPage.orphanedNote: The controller answered and no longer lists this site. The imported inventory is kept as it was; pair again to resume.
siteExtPage.deleteExtension: Delete this extension and its imported inventory
siteExtPage.helpBaseUrl: Scheme, host and port — https://unifi.example.net:443. The controller must be reachable from this meshcraft controller.
siteExtPage.helpToken: A UniFi OS API key, created in the controller under Settings → Admins. It is sealed in the credential vault and never shown again. Leave this field empty when editing to keep the stored token.
siteExtPage.helpVerifyTls: On-premise UniFi OS ships a self-signed certificate, so this is usually off. Leaving it off is a recorded choice on this controller alone, not a global relaxation.
siteExtPage.helpRemoteSite: Pick it by name. What gets stored is the stable identifier behind that name, so renaming the site on the controller does not break the pairing.
siteExtPage.revealLogged: This access has been recorded in the site log.
siteExtPage.authorityTitle: An extension mirrors, and holds no intention
siteExtPage.authorityNote: meshcraft mirrors the inventory of the controller you name here and stores no configuration of its own for it — so it never watches a setting for drift and never pushes one back. It can ask that controller to adopt a box, let one go, or push its own configuration again. It can also edit the site's SSIDs through it, because the controller lets one service set be re-read on its own and so a change can be verified; per-box settings it cannot, because that same API exposes no resource for them. What it never does is keep a second opinion about one box: two opinions do not raise an error, they silently revert each other.

sites.domainHelp: Pushed onto equipment at provisioning; the switch carries it in its own FQDN afterwards. Leave empty if this site has no domain — connectors that require one fall back to their own default.
sites.slugHelp: First path segment for this site, e.g. /lab/equipment. Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only.
sites.slugOnCreateNote: The URL slug is derived from the name on create; you can change it later.

spanningTreePage.emptyPreferred: (empty — meshcraft leaves this site's spanning tree alone)
spanningTreePage.emptyPreferredWarning: Deliberately empty: applies send NOTHING spanning-tree related to this site — no mode, no MST region, and no per-port intent (portfast/edge, BPDU guard, path cost), because they all travel on the same plan. If this site uses MST the region also stops being re-homogenised when the VLAN list changes: devices keep the old region, 802.1s silently demotes them to ordinary RSTP neighbours, and they keep forwarding and reading "ok" while it happens. Double-click a mode in Available to hand the tree back to meshcraft; a single-device push from the STP panel still works meanwhile.
spanningTreePage.help: On apply, each device receives the first preferred mode its driver advertises. Select a mode then Add (or double-click). STP is often already in Preferred by default — Drop it first if you need to move it.
spanningTreePage.mstHelp: The identity this site applies to every device running MSTP. Three values, compared exactly.
spanningTreePage.mstNameDerived: derived from the site identifier, which nothing can rename
spanningTreePage.mstNamePinned: pinned in the site plan — changing it ejects every device still carrying the old name
spanningTreePage.mstNotObserved: This is what an apply would write, computed from the site's VLAN list — not a reading of the equipment. A device not re-applied since the VLAN list last changed carries something else.
spanningTreePage.mstTipIdentity: A region is not a label. 802.1s compares the region name, the revision and a digest computed over the whole VLAN-to-instance table, and two switches are in the same region only if all three match exactly.
spanningTreePage.mstTipRename: So changing any of them on one switch does not rename its region — it REMOVES that switch from the region. It becomes its own region, the MST boundaries move and the topology is recomputed. Nothing logs it: the ports keep forwarding and the device stays green.
spanningTreePage.mstTipVlans: The digest covers every VLAN, which is why adding or removing a site VLAN changes the region. Any device not re-applied afterwards stays in the old one — re-apply spanning tree across the whole site after a VLAN change.
spanningTreePage.readOnly: Read-only on this site — site admin rights required to change the preference.
spanningTreePage.rootsDanger: TWO ROOT BRIDGES ON ONE TREE
spanningTreePage.rootsHelp: Designate which switches win the spanning-tree root election. A SECOND root on the same tree means two separate trees, and meshcraft will filter BPDUs on the path between them.
spanningTreePage.rootsMultiInstance: {{count}} root bridges, each on its own MST instance. That is ordinary MST: separate trees, nothing filtered.
spanningTreePage.rootsNoPath: meshcraft knows NO path between these root bridges, so it will filter nothing — and they may still be merged into one tree by a cable it cannot see. Declare the link, or check the neighbour table.
spanningTreePage.rootsWillFilter: {{ports}} interface(s) on {{devices}} switch(es) will stop taking part in spanning tree. They are listed below, before anything is written.

stpRegion.cannotJoinNote: This platform's connector does not write an MST region, so there is no gesture to offer here: this switch stays a region of its own and takes no part in the site's MST tree. It keeps forwarding, so nothing else will look wrong. Bringing it in is a platform decision, not a click.
stpRegion.confirmCost: This recalculates the spanning-tree topology. Ports go back through listening and learning: measured on this fleet, 2 to 5 seconds unreachable and about 45 seconds to settle. On a switch that is root of its tree, or that carries MST boundary ports, the recalculation reaches its neighbours too.
stpRegion.confirmIdentity: The region name written here becomes "{{want}}", replacing "{{have}}". Every switch still carrying the old name is in a different region from this one until it is conformed in turn — so on a fleet already split, the ORDER of these gestures is a plan, not a detail.
stpRegion.confirmModeChange: This switch does not run MSTP today, so the protocol itself changes. On some ranges that command closes the management session before the CLI answers and leaves the tree unreadable for tens of seconds.
stpRegion.conformTitle: Put this switch in the MST region its site designed
stpRegion.conformedToast: Spanning tree conformed on this switch
stpRegion.identityNote: 802.1s decides region membership on three values together — the name, the revision, and a digest over the whole VLAN-to-instance table. A bridge differing in any one of them has not been relabelled: it has LEFT the region, it keeps forwarding, and nothing reports it. Here is each value, as the site wants it and as this switch carries it.
stpRegion.observedNote: Compared against the last reading taken from this switch, not a live query. A switch that has never been read produces no verdict at all — the absence of this banner is not proof of conformity.
stpRegion.readOnlyNote: Read-only on this site: conforming the spanning tree needs site administrator rights.

switchDetailPage.stpSuperRootTitle: Writes priority 0 on MST instance 0 — nothing sorts below it, so this switch wins the root election and keeps winning it. The cost: a second Super Root in the same region is settled by MAC address, not by you, and the root can no longer be moved by raising anyone else's priority. There is no recorded undo — clearing the box asks you for a priority to put back.

switchDetailPage.networkHelp1: The network is the address domain: the space where this IP designates one machine and only one.
switchDetailPage.networkHelp2: Useful when two proxies see the same private range (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24): same network → one device; distinct networks → two devices. On a single-network instance this row stays hidden.
switchDetailPage.networkTitle: The network where this device's address makes sense. It decides which proxy may legitimately monitor it.
switchDetailPage.addressHelp1: This is the IP meshcraft uses to reach the device (ping, SNMP, apply, re-read). It is not the DHCP/static decision — that lives under "Management network".
switchDetailPage.addressHelp2: Edit it when you changed the address by hand on the switch, at adoption, or during renumbering — otherwise meshcraft keeps talking to the old IP.
switchDetailPage.addressHelp3: When meshcraft itself applies addressing, it updates this field automatically.
switchDetailPage.collectorHelp1: The reference proxy that polls this device via SNMP and should receive its traps.
switchDetailPage.collectorHelp2: With no collector chosen, any proxy covering the site may collect. With several covering proxies, this picks which one does it. Only proxies covering this site can be designated.
switchDetailPage.collectorSelectTitle: The proxy that polls this device via SNMP and receives its traps. With no designated collector, any proxy covering the site handles it. Only proxies covering this site may be designated.

switchDetailPage.monitoringGapsTitleOne: One monitoring metric is not exposed by this platform
switchDetailPage.monitoringGapsHelp1: This is not delayed collection: the device does not publish these values. No meshcraft version will make them appear here.
switchDetailPage.monitoringGapsHelp2: This list only documents absences for this model. A metric missing on screen without being listed may still be uncollected or unverified on this hardware.
switchDetailPage.absenceObservedTitle: Verified on hardware of this product line
switchDetailPage.absenceAssumedTitle: Inferred from product-line documentation, not verified on hardware
switchDetailPage.absenceAssumedWarning: No one has verified this on hardware yet: another model in the line, or newer firmware, may disprove it. If you observe the opposite, update the connector declaration.
switchDetailPage.tagsHelp1: Tagging does not touch the device. However, a site credential may target a tag: the device then falls under that expected password until an explicit push.
switchDetailPage.tagsHelpTechnical: Technical tags are placed by meshcraft from what this platform's connector declares, and are not removable. They decide credentials the device receives: snmpv3-… for supervision identity, pwpolicy-… for admin password when the platform policy rejects the site secret. They survive rule re-evaluation; matching credentials appear under Configuration → Credentials.
switchDetailPage.tagsHelpRule: Dotted tags are inferred from a site rule: removing them here only lasts until the next re-evaluation. To remove them permanently, change the rule (Tags page).
switchDetailPage.tagAppliedToast: Tag "{{tag}}" applied — nothing was changed on the device
switchDetailPage.tagRemovedRuleToast: "{{tag}}" removed — a site rule will reapply it on next re-evaluation
switchDetailPage.noTrafficNote: No traffic measurements on this port. Interface counters come from SNMP collection: without a designated collector or responding agent, there is nothing to chart — not the same as an idle port.
switchDetailPage.portClassAllUndeclared: This platform does not report traffic by class.
switchDetailPage.portClassCapsUnknown: unknown — no connector for this device
switchDetailPage.unreachableConfigNote: Switch unreachable — configuration unavailable. Last known state shown.
switchDetailPage.engineerProfilesNote: Profiles defined by the network engineer. Greyed entries are engineer-only.
switchDetailPage.cfgModeHelp1: A port is configured in one of two ways. Group: the port follows a VLAN group (a port profile) — apply it once, and the panel remembers which group this port belongs to. Manual: VLAN values set on this port alone.
switchDetailPage.cfgModeHelp2: Switching the selector changes nothing by itself: the stored configuration only moves when you apply a group or edit a manual value.
switchDetailPage.cfgModeHelp3: The first manual VLAN edit detaches the port from its group. PoE and spanning-tree adjustments do not — they are per-port overrides on top of the group, and the panel flags them as such.
switchDetailPage.groupNoneNote: This port follows no group yet — pick one below and apply.
switchDetailPage.groupDanglingNote: The group this port followed no longer exists. Its last applied configuration is kept; pick a new group, or edit values in manual mode.
switchDetailPage.manualDetachNote: Editing a VLAN value here detaches the port from the group “{{name}}”.
switchDetailPage.groupFollowedNoteMulti: These {{count}} ports all follow the group “{{name}}”.
switchDetailPage.groupNoneNoteMulti: None of these ports follows a group yet — pick one below and apply to attach them all.
switchDetailPage.groupDanglingNoteMulti: The group these ports followed no longer exists. Their last applied configuration is kept; pick a new group, or edit values in manual mode.
switchDetailPage.groupMixedNoteMulti: This selection mixes ports that follow different groups — or none. Applying a group below attaches all {{count}} selected ports to it.
switchDetailPage.manualDetachNoteMulti: Editing a VLAN value here detaches the {{count}} still-attached ports from their groups.

switchDetailPage.poeOverrideMultiRemovedToast_other: {{count}} ports follow their group's PoE setting again

switchDetailPage.taggedMembersHelp: On a selection, only full replacement makes sense: per-port tagged members are set by selecting a single port.
switchDetailPage.configReadTitle: When a connector last read this device's configuration. The sheet refreshes itself as changes arrive — this says how old the reading behind it is.
switchDetailPage.configReadBlindTitle: This reading has stopped arriving: no proxy able to watch this device is connected right now. The screen shows the last configuration read, and it will not advance until a proxy is back.
switchDetailPage.offMgmtPlan: Not on the site management plan

switchDetailPage.opticsHelp1: The module measures itself: transmitted and received optical power, temperature, supply voltage and laser bias current. meshcraft reads them when the device is re-read (⟳), not continuously — these are the values of the last read, not a live feed.
switchDetailPage.opticsHelp2: No value here is judged. The module also carries its own alarm and warning thresholds, and meshcraft does not read them, so nothing on this panel can say whether a reading is in range. Compare against the transceiver's datasheet.
switchDetailPage.opticsHelp3: A missing reading is shown as “not served”, never as a zero: 0 dBm is a legitimate optical power, and a module that reports nothing is not a module reporting zero.
switchDetailPage.opticsBlindNote: This cage could not be read on the last device read: what is in it, if anything, is unknown. Re-read the device (⟳) to find out.
switchDetailPage.opticsNoDdmNote: This module declares no diagnostics (DDM: no): it has nothing to measure itself with. Only a DDM module reports power, temperature and bias current.
switchDetailPage.vlanManualElsewhereNote: Per-port VLAN values are edited under Profile → Manual.
switchDetailPage.vlanViewerNote: Changing per-port VLANs is a network engineer gesture; the values above are what this port carries.
switchDetailPage.profileManualLaneNote: Manual lane selected: VLAN values are edited in the VLAN section. Switch back to Group to attach a profile.
switchDetailPage.snoopHelp1: The only per-port setting is TRUST: whether DHCP server replies (OFFER, ACK) arriving on this jack are accepted. Untrusted is the protected state, and it is every platform's default.
switchDetailPage.snoopHelp2: Trust the uplink toward the real DHCP server, or toward another switch — the exception, never the rule. A trusted user port lets anything plugged into it hand out addresses to the whole VLAN.
switchDetailPage.snoopHelp3: The switch-wide feature and the VLANs it inspects are the connector's business: they are turned on server-side from the site plan. This screen never sends a VLAN list.
switchDetailPage.snoopHelp4: The toggle records the decision; the button next to it writes it to the equipment now. Two gestures on purpose — a device that refuses the write must not cost you the recorded decision.
switchDetailPage.snoopWriteTitle: Push the recorded trust flag to the equipment now. The VLANs are resolved by the server from the site plan.
switchDetailPage.snoopSplitNote: The toggle records the intent; the button writes it to the equipment now.
switchDetailPage.snoopDeviceOffNote: Device-wide DHCP snooping is OFF: a trust flag protects nothing here — the switch inspects no DHCP traffic. An immediate write turns the feature on as part of the same gesture.
switchDetailPage.snoopDeviceOnNote: Device-wide snooping is on, inspecting VLAN {{vlans}}.
switchDetailPage.snoopDeviceOnNoVlanNote: Device-wide snooping is on, but it inspects no VLAN yet.
switchDetailPage.snoopDeviceUnreadHelp: Nothing on this card comes from the equipment: neither the switch-wide feature nor the per-port trust flags have ever been read. A device read (⟳) reports both.
switchDetailPage.snoopAppliedToast: DHCP snooping trust written on {{count}} port(s)
switchDetailPage.stormIntro: Discard broadcast, multicast or unknown-unicast frames on this port once they pass a threshold. Every threshold carries its unit: the same number means a percentage of line rate on one platform and packets per second on another, and nothing is ever converted between the two.
switchDetailPage.stormReadCost: Reading this opens a session on the switch. Nothing is cached — some ranges grant only four or five sessions in total.
switchDetailPage.stormReadBtn: Read storm control from the device
switchDetailPage.stormClass_unknown_unicast: Unknown unicast (flooded, destination not in the MAC table)
switchDetailPage.stormObservedNone: No limiter configured on this port.
switchDetailPage.stormForeignClass: Not read, but something IS limiting this class — the device carries:
switchDetailPage.stormForeignPortNote: This statement is not one of the three classes above: it acts on every frame crossing the port, so it limits broadcast, multicast and unknown unicast whatever the per-class settings say. meshcraft neither wrote it nor removes it.
switchDetailPage.stormForeignPortTitle: This port carries a limiter meshcraft does not model
switchDetailPage.stormObservedUnread: Not read: the connector could not establish this class, which is not the same as “no limiter”.
switchDetailPage.stormCapsUnknown: The connector for this equipment could not be resolved, so nothing can be said either way.
switchDetailPage.stormClassUnsupported: This platform has no limiter for this traffic class. Nothing is coming: writing the nearest one instead would throttle a different set of frames while the screen said otherwise.
switchDetailPage.stormNotVerified: The hardware carries this limiter, but the command form has not been run on this range yet — so the control is not offered. The first exercise must be a lab switch, not a customer's.
switchDetailPage.stormNoUnit: This platform declares no rate unit, so no threshold can be sent.
switchDetailPage.stormSharedRate: This platform stores ONE rate per port, shared by every class limited on it.
switchDetailPage.stormSharedConflict: Two different thresholds ({{a}} and {{b}}) on a port that stores only one: neither would be written. Use one value, or apply the classes in two gestures.
switchDetailPage.stormApplyBtn: Apply storm control to this port
switchDetailPage.stormDraftInvalid: A threshold is missing, is zero, or is not a whole count for its unit. A threshold of zero drops every frame of the class — to remove a limiter, untick it.
switchDetailPage.selectionHelpClear: Click the background, or press Escape, to clear the selection.
switchDetailPage.selectionHelpDouble: Double-click a port to open its actions: shut / bring back up, and PoE power cycle.
switchDetailPage.portActionIntro: Both gestures reach the equipment immediately. Neither is a stored configuration: nothing here is reconciled, and a later apply will not repeat it.
switchDetailPage.portActionShutWhat: Shutting the port stops it forwarding: whatever is plugged into it loses the network until the port is brought back up from here.
switchDetailPage.portActionEnableWhat: This port is administratively shut. Bringing it back up lets the link come up again — the switch decides how long that takes.
switchDetailPage.portActionAdminUnsupported: This platform does not declare port administrative state as writable: the gesture would reach nothing.
switchDetailPage.portActionLinkWarnTitle: This port carries a live link
switchDetailPage.portActionLinkWarnBody: Shutting it drops that link now. On the ranges with neither SSH nor a serial port, shutting the jack that carries the administration session ends the session for good, and the only way back is a visit on site.
switchDetailPage.portActionForceCheck: I know what this port carries — shut it anyway
switchDetailPage.portActionCycleBody: Cuts the power for {{seconds}} s, then restores it: the powered device REBOOTS. This is not a link bounce — a camera or an access point on this jack restarts and comes back in its own time.
switchDetailPage.portActionCycleWaitNote: The answer arrives once power is back: that is what proves the restore half worked. Do not reload.
switchDetailPage.portActionCycleNoPoe: This jack sources no power: there is nothing to cycle.
switchDetailPage.portActionCycleUnsupported: This platform does not declare PoE as writable: no power cycle here.
switchDetailPage.portAdminReadNote: Nothing is stored: the faceplate keeps showing the last state read from the equipment until the next re-read (⟳).
switchDetailPage.portCycleDoneToast: PoE cycled on {{port}} — power is back
switchDetailPage.hostnameHelp1: There is one name, not two: the name above is also the name the equipment itself answers with — its console banner, its LLDP system-name TLV, and every syslog line it emits at three in the morning.
switchDetailPage.hostnameHelp2: meshcraft keeps the two in step on its own: if the equipment stops carrying that name, it is written back automatically, so there is nothing to press here. The only case that needs you is a name that cannot be a hostname at all — accents and punctuation are refused, spaces are no problem.
switchDetailPage.hostnameOk: The equipment answers to this name.
switchDetailPage.hostnameDrift: The equipment answers to “{{observed}}”; meshcraft is already putting “{{desired}}” back on it.
switchDetailPage.hostnameNotObserved: Not reported yet: nothing has told meshcraft which name this equipment carries.
switchDetailPage.hostnameUnsupported: meshcraft cannot write a name onto this platform: the equipment keeps the name it carries.
switchDetailPage.hostnameUnnameable: This name cannot become a hostname, so no name is being written onto the equipment. Rename the device using letters, digits and hyphens only.
switchDetailPage.portActionCapsUnknown: meshcraft could not resolve this device's connector, so it cannot say which port actions the platform allows. The buttons stay out of the way rather than promise a gesture that may reach nothing.

wifiPage.ssidsHelp: An SSID is configured on the site and broadcast by every access point, so it belongs to the site rather than to one box. No passphrase is imported.
wifiPage.adoptableHelp: Adopting asks the controller to take a box into the paired site. The box then gets the site's configuration from the controller, not from meshcraft. It takes a minute or two to finish, so a freshly adopted box shows as adopting before it shows as online.
wifiPage.adoptableScopeTitle: These boxes belong to no site yet
wifiPage.adoptableScopeNote: A box awaiting adoption is not assigned anywhere, so the controller offers the same list whichever site you ask from — including boxes standing at another venue. Adopting is what attaches one to this site. Check the address before you do.
wifiPage.adopted: Adoption asked for; the controller takes a minute or two
wifiPage.reprovision: Ask the controller to push its configuration to {{name}} again
wifiPage.forgetTitle: Remove a box from the controller
wifiPage.forgetWarnTitle: This removes “{{name}}” and cannot be undone
wifiPage.forgetWarnNote: The box leaves the site, resets itself and returns to awaiting adoption. Its name and anything configured on it specifically are lost. Re-adopting brings it back as a new box — it does not restore them. If it cannot reach the controller afterwards, somebody has to go to it.
wifiPage.forgetFieldHelp: Type it as the controller reports it right now. It is re-read and compared at the moment of the call, so a box that has been renamed, replaced or is not the one you think it is will refuse instead of being destroyed.
wifiPage.rightsUnprovenTip: The token belongs to {{admin}}, who is neither owner nor super-admin. The controller does not say what it may do per site, so these gestures may be refused — they are offered rather than hidden, because a right we cannot read is not a right we can deny.
wifiPage.mirrorAgeTip: The controller is read in the background every 30 seconds. This list is what the last successful read returned — not what the controller holds this instant.
wifiPage.apsReadOnlyHelpLabel: Why these boxes have no settings
wifiPage.apsReadOnlyHelp: The SSIDs above can be edited; these access points cannot, and that is a limit of the controller rather than a restriction here. Its API exposes no per-box configuration resource, so there is nowhere to send a channel or a name — and the readings that remain omit any setting left at its default, so a write could not be verified even if one landed. Changing a per-box setting is still a visit to the UniFi interface. What can be asked of the controller is to re-push its own configuration, or to let a box go.
wifiPage.ssidEditHowTitle: Sent to the controller, then read back
wifiPage.ssidEditHowNote: These values were just read from the controller, not from the list behind this dialog. Saving sends only what you change, and only if the controller still holds the value shown here — if somebody edited this SSID meanwhile, nothing is sent and you are told what it is now. Nothing is kept here afterwards: meshcraft holds no setting of its own, so it never watches one for drift and never pushes one back.
wifiPage.ssidEditLoading: Reading this SSID from the controller…
wifiPage.ssidNameHelp: The network name clients see. Renaming it disconnects everyone associated, who will have to join the new name.
wifiPage.ssidSecurityFrozen: Shown, not editable. The combination of keys WPA3 requires could not be established without writing to a controller in service, and a guessed one takes a network off the air. To rotate the key, change the passphrase below — the security mode stays as it is.
wifiPage.ssidPassphraseHelp: Write-only. It is deliberately shown empty rather than as masked dots that would look like a value: leave it empty and the current passphrase is kept exactly as it is. Type one and it replaces the old one, which disconnects every associated client. meshcraft never displays or stores the current passphrase.
wifiPage.ssidPassphraseKeep: leave empty to keep the current one
wifiPage.ssidNetworkHelp: The controller's network, which carries the VLAN this SSID's traffic lands on. Changing it moves every associated client.
wifiPage.ssidNetworkUnavailable: the controller did not return its network list; this field cannot be changed right now
wifiPage.ssidBandsHelp: The radio bands this SSID is offered on. Turning off a band disconnects the clients using it.
wifiPage.ssidBandsLocked: this SSID carries a band this version cannot write, so its bands are left alone rather than silently narrowed
wifiPage.ssidSwitchUnknown: the controller does not report this setting, so there is nothing to compare a change against

profilePage.title: My profile
profilePage.noSiteRole: No role on any site yet.
profilePage.identityReadOnly: Your name, email and password are changed by a global administrator, from Configuration › Users.
profilePage.ruleTitle: A token authenticates you. It does not grant you anything.
profilePage.ruleNote: A token is a second way of proving who you are, and it is worth exactly your own rights at the moment of the call — never more. Its scope can only reduce them. Lose a role, and every one of your tokens loses it in the same second.
profilePage.noTokens: No token yet. Only you can create, see or revoke yours — not even a global administrator can.
profilePage.revokedToast: Token revoked. It no longer authenticates anything.
profilePage.createHelp: The scope below applies ON TOP of your own rights, never in their place. A read-only token held by a site administrator still refuses every write; a read-write token held by a viewer still reads only. The defaults are deliberately the least powerful ones.
profilePage.nameHelp: The only free text on a token, and the only thing that will tell you months from now whether it can be revoked. Name the thing that uses it, not the person.
profilePage.readOnlyHint: Refuses every write, whatever you are allowed to do. Leave it on unless the script has to change something.
profilePage.expiryHelp: A lost token is as serious as your password, minus the scope it gave itself. An expiry is what bounds that, including for the token you forget you created.
profilePage.sitesHelp: Among the sites you can already reach. Leave it empty and the token reaches all of them — which is the widest token this product mints.
profilePage.allSitesWarnTitle: This token will reach every site you can
profilePage.allSitesWarnBody: No site chosen means no restriction, not no access. Pick at least one unless you really mean the whole fleet.
profilePage.willBeAbleTo: This token will be able to
profilePage.secretWarnTitle: This value will never be shown again
profilePage.secretWarnBody: It is stored hashed, exactly like a session. Nobody — not the server, not a global administrator, not this page if you reload it — can show it to you a second time. Copy it now; if you lose it, revoke the token and create another.
profilePage.savedByHand: I have written it down myself
profilePage.secretHeaderOnly: It travels in the Authorization header and nowhere else — never in a cookie, never in a URL, never in a query string.
profilePage.sessionOnlyNote: Creating and revoking a token need your signed-in session — a token cannot do either, by design. Everything else on this product's API, a token can do, because it is the same handler.
profilePage.secretPrefix: In the list it will show as
profilePage.capNote: Twenty active tokens is the cap and the server refuses the next one. It is a hygiene limit, not a security one: this list is the revocation tool, and a list nobody reads is a list nobody acts on. Revoke what the "last used" column says nothing uses.

apiDocs.title: API reference
apiDocs.subtitle: The HTTP interface this product's own frontend uses — and the one your scripts use, through the same handlers.
apiDocs.sourceNote: There is no specification file for this API. The table below is written by hand, read off internal/api/api.go and its handlers, and no build step can check it. The two boundaries that DO have a machine-served OpenAPI specification are the driver protocol and the controller↔proxy lifeline — those are below, and the product serves them itself.
apiDocs.sourceCaveat: It is also a selection, not the whole router: the per-device action routes and the discovery subtree are described by their group and their authorization gate rather than listed one by one. When a path here disagrees with the product, the product is right.
apiDocs.authBody: One header, on every request. The token is the whole credential: there is no login call to make first and no session to keep.
apiDocs.neverCookieBody: The token travels in the Authorization header and nowhere else. That is what makes it immune to CSRF: a browser does not send a header on its own. Putting it in a cookie would hand every page on the internet the ability to spend it on your behalf. The browser interface keeps its own session cookie and never uses a token — the trade runs the other way round than it looks.
apiDocs.can1: Everything you can do through the interface, because it is the same handler. There is no API "for agents" beside an API "for the frontend".
apiDocs.can2: Carry a scope that REDUCES: read-only, a list of sites, an expiry date. The scope applies on top of your rights, never in their place.
apiDocs.can3: Be revoked at any moment, from your profile, with immediate effect.
apiDocs.cannot1: Grant a right its holder does not have. A viewer's token does not become an administrator by asking for it.
apiDocs.cannot2: Outlive its holder's rights. Remove someone's role and their tokens lose it in the same second, with nothing to revoke one by one.
apiDocs.cannot3: Reach another user's tokens. There is no route that takes a user id, for anybody, including a global administrator.
apiDocs.cannot4: Be read back. The clear value exists once, in the response that created it, and is stored hashed.
apiDocs.adrPointer: The rule and the alternatives that were rejected are written down in ADR-0011, "A token authenticates, it does not authorise".
apiDocs.securityIntro: A token is a password with a scope. It opens a product that configures network equipment, so the worst case is not a data leak: it is somebody reaching a switch. Everything below follows from that one sentence.
apiDocs.dont1: Do not commit it. Not in a repository, not in a Dockerfile, not in a CI definition, not in a Helm values file — a private repository is one fork away from being a public one.
apiDocs.dont2: Do not type it on a command line. It lands in the shell history of whoever pasted it, and in the process list of everybody on the machine while the command runs. Read it from an environment variable or a file instead.
apiDocs.dont3: Do not put it in a URL, a query string or a path. Those are logged by every proxy on the way, kept by the browser's history, and sent in the Referer header.
apiDocs.dont4: Do not share one between two things. A token shared by a script and a colleague identifies nobody: the event log would say "somebody deleted this VLAN".
apiDocs.dont5: Do not give it write access it does not need. Most automation reads; a read-only token that leaks cannot take a site down.
apiDocs.dont6: Do not make it immortal. "Never expires" exists for the rare case that needs it, and every one of those cases eventually becomes a token nobody remembers issuing.
apiDocs.browserTitle: Why it does not belong in a browser
apiDocs.browserBody: Storing a long-lived token in a page is strictly worse than the session cookie this interface uses. A HttpOnly cookie is out of reach of JavaScript; a token in localStorage is readable by any cross-site scripting flaw on any page of the origin, and it does not expire on its own. If you are writing something that runs in a browser against this API, the answer is the session, not a token.
apiDocs.do1: One token per consumer, named after the consumer. That is what makes the event log and the "last used" column able to answer a question.
apiDocs.do2: Keep it in the secret store you already have — the CI's secret, a systemd credential, a file readable only by the service account.
apiDocs.do3: Serve this product over TLS. The header is plaintext on the wire like everything else; there is nothing in a token that protects itself.
apiDocs.do4: Revoke on a schedule rather than on an incident. A token nobody can tell is still in use is a token nobody dares revoke — which is why the "last used" column exists.
apiDocs.leakIntro: In this order, and the first step is the only one that stops the bleeding.
apiDocs.leak1: Revoke it, from your profile. It stops authenticating immediately — there is no cache and no grace period.
apiDocs.leak2: Create a replacement and deploy it. Do it second: a service that breaks is a service somebody is tempted to un-revoke.
apiDocs.leak3: Read the instance event log for what it did while it was out. A write by a token is a write by you, under your name.
apiDocs.leak4: Assume everything the token could reach is compromised, not just what the log shows. If it was read-write on all your sites, that includes the equipment credentials it could deploy.
apiDocs.versioningBody: /api/v1/ means exactly two things: the agent lifeline and the contract documents. Everything else is unversioned /api/… and may move — pin nothing, read the response.
apiDocs.paginationBody: There is none. Collection routes return a bare JSON array of everything in scope; a few accept a limit query parameter. Site scoping is in the path, never in a query parameter.
apiDocs.tabHeaderBody: Optional, on writes. Any identifier of your choosing; the server uses it so that the live-change stream does not echo your own write back to you. It authenticates nothing and lying about it only costs you the refresh.
apiDocs.envelopeBody: Exactly one field, on every failure. There is no code, no details, no nested object. Show the sentence to the operator verbatim: it is written to be read, and it often names the repair.
apiDocs.envelopeQuirk: Two exceptions worth knowing: the 401 for a missing session and the 403 from the global-administrator gate are written as plain text, so they carry Content-Type: text/plain and a trailing newline despite the JSON body. Parse defensively.

code.200: Done. The body is the resource, or {"status":"ok"}.
code.201: Created. The body is the new resource, with its id.
code.202: Accepted and started in the background — a build, a scan. Poll the resource.
code.400: Your request is wrong: a missing field, a bad value, malformed JSON.
code.401: No valid credential. Your token is absent, unknown, revoked or expired.
code.403: Authenticated, not allowed. Your role on that site, or your token's scope, refuses it.
code.404: No such row — or, on an unknown /api/ path, no such route, for any verb.
code.409: A conflict with what is already there: a duplicate, or a protected object such as VLAN 1.
code.413: Body too large. The cap is 1 MiB, and 8 MiB for a site configuration import.
code.422: This API's signature code: your request is well-formed and the fleet refuses it anyway — no proxy covers that site, no collector is declared, external drivers are off on this instance. The message names the repair.
code.429: Too many of these, too fast. Wait and retry.
code.500: A fault on our side. The message is usually just "internal error"; the cause is in the server log.
code.502: A device or a driver answered badly, or stopped answering mid-write. Read the body: a half-applied write names what it could not put back.
code.503: A dependency is down — the database, typically. Nothing you sent is at fault.

apiDocs.queryBody: The complete list for the whole API. A parameter that is not here does not exist, and an unparseable value is silently ignored rather than refused.
apiDocs.quickstartNote: Against this instance, with a token from your profile. Five calls, chained: prove the token, find a site, read it, write to it.

gd.apiTokens: The three routes of ADR-0011, under /api/auth/ with the session and the SOCKS token — where a credential belongs. The list is readable by a token; CREATING AND REVOKING ARE NOT, because a token able to mint another one would outlive its own expiry and its own revocation. Nobody sees anybody else's tokens, not even a global administrator: there is no route that takes a user id.
gd.session: The browser's door. A token does not use /api/auth/login and does not need to: /api/auth/me answers it directly, and is the cheapest way to check that a token still works.
gd.sites: A site is the unit of authorization in this product: almost every other route resolves to one and asks CanSite about it. The list is already filtered to what you can reach, so it is also the answer to "what does this token see".
gd.vlans: The smallest complete example in this API — a list, a create, a patch, a delete, with a real guard on VLAN 1. Worth reading first if you are writing a client.
gd.devices: There is deliberately no GET /api/devices/{id}: the hostname-conformity verdict is published only by the site list, so a single-device read would answer with a different truth. PATCH MERGES — an absent field keeps its stored value, and an explicit null is the only way to clear one.
gd.ports: Two different things, and confusing them is the commonest mistake against this API. A PUT on /ports stores INTENT and touches no hardware — reconciliation applies it later. The /apply and /admin routes WRITE TO THE DEVICE now, synchronously, and leave nothing behind for reconciliation to maintain.
gd.siteReads: What a read-only token is for. /stream is server-sent events, not JSON — open it with an event-source client and pass the same identifier you send as X-Meshcraft-Tab.
gd.users: Global administrator only, the whole subtree. Note what is NOT here: nobody reaches anybody's API tokens through these routes, and a PATCH ignores the email field entirely.
gd.instance: The fleet-wide screens. Proxies and discovery prefixes are gated by COVERAGE rather than by a single site — you administer a proxy when you administer every site it covers.
gd.contracts: The two boundaries that DO have a specification, served by the product itself and anonymous because the code on the other side has no session. Read those documents rather than this page for anything a driver or a proxy does.
gd.anon: The complete list, and it is short on purpose. Each one is here for a caller that cannot have a session: a load balancer, a driver author, the holder of a dashboard share link, a proxy fetching its own image. If you are auditing this deployment, this is the list to audit.

r.listTokens: Your own active tokens, newest first — a bare array, empty when you hold none. It carries `prefix`, the visible head of each value, which is how you tell two tokens apart. It never carries the value itself, and no route does.
r.createToken: Mints one, and answers the token row PLUS a `token` field flat inside it — the only response in this API that carries a usable secret, and the only moment it exists. Everything but `name` is optional, and every default is the least powerful option: read-only, 90 days, no site restriction.
r.revokeToken: Revokes one of your own, immediately — the next call with it answers 401. A 404 covers "no such token" AND "not yours", indistinguishable on purpose so the route cannot be used to probe who holds what.
r.login: For the browser. Sets the meshcraft_session cookie; a token never calls this.
r.logout: Clears the session cookie. Nothing to do with revoking a token.
r.me: Who the credential belongs to, with every site role. The cheapest way for a script to verify its token and discover its own rights.
r.socksGet: Whether you have a SOCKS route token, and where the listener is. Never reveals it.
r.socksPost: Mints a SOCKS route token, shown once. This REPLACES the previous one, which is how it is revoked.
r.version: The product version, and the UTC build stamp that answers "is my fix deployed".
r.healthz: Liveness, for a load balancer. 503 when the database is unreachable.
r.listSites: Every site you hold a role on — all of them if you are a global administrator.
r.createSite: Also creates the site's administrator credential.
r.patchSite: Name, slug and local domain. local_domain is a POINTER on the Go side: absent leaves it, an empty string clears it.
r.deleteSite: Takes the site and everything under it. Global administrator only.
r.createVlan: An empty color is filled in server-side.
r.patchVlan: The site is read from the VLAN row, not from the path.
r.deleteVlan: VLAN 1 is the site's default and is protected.
r.listDevices: The big one. Each row is the stored device plus several layers computed on read — synchronisation, drift, management conformity, optics. Those are never writable; do not send them back.
r.createDevice: status is not accepted on input: reachability is written by the watch loop and by nothing else. A catalog model pre-fills the port groups.
r.patchDevice: Merge semantics — see the group note above.
r.deleteDevice: Removes it from the model. Touches no hardware.
r.moveDevice: Needs site administrator on BOTH sites.
r.telemetry: Samples over a window, with ?minutes=. A viewer's token is enough.
r.putPort: Stores the intent for one port. The body is the port configuration ITSELF, not wrapped in a field.
r.putPorts: The same, for a selection. 512 ports maximum, one event rather than one per port.
r.configApply: Writes the stored intent to the device, now. Opens a session on the hardware.
r.portsAdmin: Brings ports up or down on the hardware immediately. Leaves nothing in the model and nothing reconciles it back.
r.powerCycle: Cuts PoE and restores it. BLOCKS for the off-delay, and a failed restore reports which port stayed dark in the error body — read it.
r.readState: Reads the device now and refreshes what meshcraft believes about it.
r.lldp: The site's neighbours, the links deduced from them, and the devices that say nothing.
r.clients: Learned MAC addresses, located and identified.
r.traffic: Per-port counters over a window, with ?hours=.
r.stream: Server-sent events: "this site changed". Not JSON.
r.export: The whole site configuration as one JSON attachment.
r.import: Takes that file back. Refuses as a whole rather than half-applying.
r.siteCreds: The equipment credentials, WITHOUT their secrets — only has_secret booleans. Revealing one is a separate, audited call.
r.listUsers: Every account, with its site roles.
r.createUser: Password of at least eight characters.
r.patchUser: An empty password leaves it unchanged. You cannot demote yourself.
r.deleteUser: You cannot delete your own account.
r.putRoles: Replaces the whole role list. The body is a BARE ARRAY, not an object.
r.events: The instance log — logins and instance-wide credentials land here.
r.proxies: Filtered to the proxies that cover a site you can see, plus the instance ones.
r.candidates: What discovery found and nobody has adopted. ?adopted=1 includes the rest.
r.adopt: Turns a candidate into equipment on a site you choose in the body.
r.driverRepos: The git repositories built into driver containers the controller RUNS.
r.agentRepos: The git repositories built into OCI layouts a remote proxy PULLS.
r.contractMdp: The driver protocol, OpenAPI, hand-written and authoritative.
r.contractMdpSchemas: The same, as generated JSON Schema. Never edited by hand.
r.contractAgent: The controller↔proxy lifeline: enroll, heartbeat, migrate, the metrics pushes.
r.contractAgentSchemas: The same, as generated JSON Schema.
r.agentEnroll: A proxy trades an enrolment token for its own identity. Authenticates itself in the body; /api/proxy/enroll is a permanent alias.
r.agentHeartbeat: The proxy says it is alive and gets its orders back. Credentials in the body.
r.contractAny: {name} is mdp, agent, mdp-schemas or agent-schemas. Cached five minutes.
r.publicDashboard: The one deliberately anonymous READ in the product. The token names exactly one dashboard; every field is projected by hand and the scope is closed inside the handler.
r.downloadProxy: A proxy's own installer. Anonymous because a proxy has no session yet.
r.registry: The built-in OCI registry a remote proxy pulls its image from.

apiDocs.cannot5: Mint or revoke a token. Those two need the password-backed session: a token that can create another outlives its own expiry and its own revocation.
apiDocs.refusalsIntro: A 401 means "get a new credential". A 403 means "this will never work with this credential" — retrying it by re-authenticating loops forever, which is why a read-only refusal is not a 401.
apiDocs.refusalInvalid: Malformed, unknown, or the wrong secret. The three are deliberately the same sentence: distinguishing them would tell somebody probing which half of their guess was right.
apiDocs.refusalRevoked: Somebody revoked it. There is no cache and no grace period.
apiDocs.refusalExpired: Its expiry has passed. Mint another; the old one cannot be extended.
apiDocs.refusalReadOnly: A read-only token tried to write. Your own rights are irrelevant here — the scope reduces, and it reduced this.
apiDocs.refusalSites: A token restricted to a list of sites reached for something outside it — an instance-wide subtree, or another site.
apiDocs.refusalCookieOnly: You tried to mint or revoke a token with a token. Use the signed-in session.
apiDocs.refusalCap: Twenty active tokens is the cap, and it is a hygiene limit rather than a security one: the list is the revocation tool, and a list nobody reads is a list nobody acts on. Revoke one.
